Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $[\lambda]$ be its Young diagram
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A **tableau of shape
$\lambda$**, or $\lambda$-tableau, is a bijection
$$t:[\lambda]\longrightarrow\{1,2,\dots,n\}.$$
We write $t(i,j)$ for the entry of $t$ in the node $(i,j)$, and we display $t$
as the diagram $[\lambda]$ with each node carrying its entry. Thus a tableau
places each of the numbers $1,\dots,n$ in exactly one node of $[\lambda]$. For
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the diagram is empty and the empty map is the unique
tableau of shape $\varnothing$, the **empty tableau**. The **shape** of a
tableau $t$ is the partition $\lambda$ with $t:[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$,
which is determined by $t$ because $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$.

**Standard tableaux.** A tableau $t$ of shape $\lambda$ is **standard** if its
entries strictly increase along rows and down columns, that is, if
$$t(i,j)<t(i,j+1)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i,j+1)\in[\lambda],$$
$$t(i,j)<t(i+1,j)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i+1,j)\in[\lambda].$$
The empty tableau is standard, because both conditions are vacuous, and it is
the unique standard tableau of shape $\varnothing$. Following the classical
notation we write $f^\lambda$ for the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux.

**The left action on tableaux.** For $\sigma\in S_n$ and a $\lambda$-tableau
$t$, define
$$(\sigma\cdot t)(i,j):=\sigma\bigl(t(i,j)\bigr)\qquad\bigl((i,j)\in[\lambda]\bigr).$$
Since $t$ is a bijection onto $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $\sigma$ is a bijection of
$\{1,\dots,n\}$, the map $\sigma\cdot t$ is again a bijection
$[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$, hence again a $\lambda$-tableau, and
$\mathrm{id}\cdot t=t$, $\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot t)=(\sigma\tau)\cdot t$ for all
$\sigma,\tau\in S_n$: the rule is a left action of $S_n$ on the set of
$\lambda$-tableaux. For every $\sigma\in S_n$ the row sets of $\sigma\cdot t$
are the images under $\sigma$ of the row sets of $t$, and the column sets of
$\sigma\cdot t$ are the images under $\sigma$ of the column sets of $t$.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

For $\sigma \in S_n$ and $0 \le p,q < n$, define the rank number

$$r_\sigma(p,q) := \big|\{\, i \in n : i \le p \text{ and } \sigma(i)\le q\,\}\big|.$$

For $\sigma,\tau \in S_n$, write

$$\sigma \le_{\mathrm{Bruhat}} \tau \quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad r_\sigma(p,q)\ge r_\tau(p,q)\ \text{for every }0 \le p,q < n.$$

This is the rank-inequality form of the Bruhat order.

Let $\le$ be the rank-inequality order on the zero-based $S_n$ of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], and identify it with the one-based realization by shifting inputs and values by $1$. (a) This order is the strong Bruhat order of type A: the transitive closure of covers $x\to tx$ where $t$ is a transposition and $\ell(tx)=\ell(x)+1$. (b) If $y\le w$ then $\ell(y)\le\ell(w)$, with equality iff $y=w$; every saturated chain has $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ steps; and $y\le w$ iff $y^{-1}\le w^{-1}$. (c) $y\le w$ iff for every reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, $y$ is a reduced subword. (d) For every simple reflection $s$, if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$, then $y\le sw$; if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$, then $sy\le w$. (e) Every interval $[y,w]$ is finite; if $y\le w$, then $[y,w]=\{y\}\cup\bigcup_{y\to a\le w}[a,w]$.

derivations.claim: **The permutation criterion.** Let $t=(a\ b)$ with $a<b$ act on values and write $p=x^{-1}(a)$, $q=x^{-1}(b)$. If $p<q$, direct inversion counting gives $\ell(tx)-\ell(x)=1+2\#\{j:p<j<q,\ a<x(j)<b\}>0$; if $p>q$ the difference is its negative. A positive difference need not equal one. The rank inequalities in [F5] show $x<tx$ precisely in the first case: the rank count decreases by one for $p\le h<q$ and $a\le k<b$, and is unchanged elsewhere. Thus every displayed earlier-node transposition lowers strong Bruhat order. Conversely a saturated strong-Bruhat chain from $w_S$ to $w_T$ consists of transposition covers by [F6], each of whose inverse lowering move has the earlier larger value by the formula just proved. Reading this chain backwards yields the displayed transposition criterion.

**Agreement outside the Garnir belt.** In the row-reading initial labelling the two pieces of the belt form one contiguous interval of positions $[L,U]$: the upper-row tail is immediately followed by the lower-row prefix. A Garnir tableau changes labels only inside this interval, so $w_T$ is in the parabolic subgroup generated by $s_L,\ldots,s_{U-1}$. Sorting its interval permutation gives a reduced expression using only these generators. The Bruhat subword criterion applied to this expression says that every $w_S\le w_T$ likewise uses only these generators. Hence $w_S$ fixes all positions outside $[L,U]$, proving agreement with $t^\mu$ outside the belt. This applies even to nonstandard $S$.

**The prefix-shape criterion.** For a row-strict $W$ and a value $c$, row-strictness makes the entries $\le c$ in each row a prefix, so $\operatorname{sh}(W^{\le c})$ is a row sequence of size $c$, and for $p=P_k+t$ with $P_k$ the number of nodes in the first $k$ rows and $0\le t<\mu_{k+1}$ we get $$N_W(p,c):=\#\{i\le p:\text{entry }i\text{ of }W\le c\}=A_k(W,c)+\min\bigl(t,s_{k+1}(W,c)\bigr),$$ where $A_k(W,c)$ is the number of entries $\le c$ in the first $k$ rows and $s_{k+1}(W,c)$ the prefix length in row $k+1$. By [F5], $w_S\le w_T$ iff $N_S(p,c)\ge N_T(p,c)$ for all $p,c$. At $p=P_k$ this says $A_k(S,c)\ge A_k(T,c)$ for all $k,c$, which is exactly $\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le c})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le c})$ for all $c$; hence the prefix criterion is necessary. Conversely assume all these prefix inequalities, fix $p=P_k+t$ and put $a=A_k(S,c)-A_k(T,c)\ge0$, $s=s_{k+1}(S,c)$, $s'=s_{k+1}(T,c)$; the inequality at $k+1$ gives $a+s\ge s'$. If $t\le s$ then $a+\min(t,s)=a+t\ge\min(t,s')$, because $t\le s'$ gives $a+t\ge t$ and $t>s'$ gives $a+t\ge t\ge s'$; if $t>s$ then $a+\min(t,s)=a+s\ge s'\ge\min(t,s')$. Thus $N_S(p,c)\ge N_T(p,c)$ for all $p,c$ and $S\unlhd T$. Since the first $k$ rows of $t^\mu$ contain $\min(c,P_k)$ entries $\le c$, the maximum possible, $\operatorname{sh}(t^{\mu\le c})$ dominates every $\operatorname{sh}(W^{\le c})$, so $t^\mu$ is the least element of $\unlhd$ on row-strict tableaux.

**Consecutive swaps and the edges of the weak graph.** Let $T$ be standard. If $r,r+1$ share a row, row-strictness puts $r$ immediately left of $r+1$ and the swap reverses an adjacent pair, so $s_rT$ is not row-strict; if they share a column, column-strictness puts $r$ immediately above $r+1$ and the swap reverses an adjacent column pair, so $s_rT$ is not column-strict. If in one component $r+1$ lies strictly above and strictly left of $r$, let $x$ be the entry of $T$ in the node in the row of $r$ and the column of $r+1$: row-strictness gives $x<r$ while column-strictness gives $x>r+1$, impossible, and symmetrically $r$ cannot lie strictly above and strictly left of $r+1$. The only remaining same-component configurations are $r
earrow_Tr+1$ and $r+1
earrow_Tr$; in either, the nodes sharing a row or column with the two positions are unchanged except for the interchange of the consecutive values $r,r+1$, so all strict neighbour inequalities survive and $s_rT$ is standard. If $r,r+1$ lie in different components the swap is standard as well. This proves the stated equivalence. For the edge criterion note that $S=s_rT$ with both standard and $r$ earlier than $r+1$ in $T$: in one component the alternatives of the equivalence leave only $r+1
earrow_Tr$ (in the other alternative $r+1$ is in a higher row and hence earlier, and same-row or same-column swaps are excluded), while in different components $r$ is earlier exactly when its component is earlier.

**Row sorting.** Let $S,T$ be $\mu$-tableaux with $S\unlhd T$; by steps 1.1 and 2.1 it suffices to treat a single transposition $S=(a\,b)T$ with $a<b$ and $b$ earlier than $a$ in $T$, the general case following by composing the finitely many single-swap comparisons. Write $S^+,T^+$ for the tableaux obtained by sorting every row increasingly. If $a,b$ share a row of $T$, then $S$ and $T$ have the same row sets and $S^+=T^+$. Otherwise the node of $b$ lies in a strictly earlier row than the node of $a$: they are in different rows by the previous sentence, and $b$ earlier than $a$ forces $b$'s row to be the earlier one. Entries other than $a,b$ occupy the same nodes in $S$ and $T$. For a value $c$, the prefix row lengths of $S^+$ and $T^+$ at $c$ are the rows' counts of entries $\le c$; if $c<a$ or $c\ge b$ these counts agree, while if $a\le c<b$ the count vector of $S^+$ is obtained from that of $T^+$ by moving one unit from the row of $a$ to the earlier row of $b$. Moving a unit to an earlier row raises every partial sum of the row sequence, so $\operatorname{sh}(S^{+\le c})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{+\le c})$ for every $c$; both tableaux are row-strict, so step 2.1 gives $S^+\unlhd T^+$. Hence $S\unlhd T$ implies $S^+\unlhd T^+$ in general.

**The vertical consecutive swap and its exceptional prefix.** Assume $\mu$ is a multipartition, $T$ standard, $r\downarrow_Tr+1$, so $r$ and $r+1$ occupy adjacent rows $a,a+1$ of one component in the same column $b$; the neighbour check of step 3.1 shows that $U:=s_rT$ is row-strict. Let $S$ be standard with $S\lhd U$; we prove $S\unlhd T$. By step 2.1, $\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le c})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le c})$ for all $c$, and for $c
e r$ the tableaux $U^{\le c}$ and $T^{\le c}$ occupy the same nodes, so their shapes agree. For $c=r$ let $A_k$ be the number of entries $\le r-1$ in the first $k$ rows of $T$ (the same for $U$) and note that $\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})$ has row lengths $A_k-A_{k-1}+[k=a+1]$ while $\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$ has $A_k-A_{k-1}+[k=a]$; thus $\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$ is obtained from $\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})$ by moving one node from row $a+1$ up to row $a$. Because $T$ is standard, the node of $r$ in row $a$ has column $b$, so exactly $b-1$ entries of row $a$ lie in columns $<b$, all of them $\le r-1$, and the same count holds in row $a+1$ whose node in column $b$ is occupied by $r+1$; hence $A_a-A_{a-1}=b-1=A_{a+1}-A_a$ and the switch hypothesis $\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})_a-\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})_{a+1}=(b-1)-((b-1)+1)=-1$ holds. **The four terminal alternatives (horizontal).** Let $\mu$ be a multipartition and $T$ be standard with $r	o_Tr+1$. Consider the three properties: (a) there is $t$ with $|t-r|>1$ such that $t
earrow_Tt+1$ or $t$ lies in a later component than $t+1$; (b) $r+1
earrow_Tr+2$ or $r+1$ lies in a later component than $r+2$; (c) $r-1
earrow_Tr$ or $r-1$ lies in a later component than $r$. By step 3.1 an incoming edge at $t$ (that is, $s_tT$ standard with $t$ earlier than $t+1$ in $s_tT$) is equivalent to $t
earrow_Tt+1$ or $t$ in a later component than $t+1$. If (a) holds, then $X:=s_tT$ is standard and $X\xrightarrow{t}T$ is an edge, so $T$ is $t$-terminal, and since $t
otin\{r,r+1\}$ the relation $r	o_Tr+1$ persists in $X$; this is alternative (1). If (b) holds with $r+1
earrow_Tr+2$, then in $X:=s_{r+1}T$ the entry $r+1$ occupies the higher node of $r+2$, so $X\xrightarrow{r+1}T$ is an edge; since $r,r+1$ are adjacent in one row and $r+2$ is above and right, $r+1$ is above and right of $r$ in $X$, so $Y:=s_rX$ is standard and $Y\xrightarrow{r}X$ is an edge with $r$ moving to the higher node, and in $Y$ the entries $r+1,r+2$ are adjacent in one row with $r+1$ to the left; this is alternative (2). If (b) holds with $r+1$ in a later component than $r+2$, the same construction with component arguments gives (2). If (c) holds, the mirror construction gives (3). It remains to observe that if none of (a),(b),(c) holds, then $T$ has no incoming edge: indeed (a) is exactly the incoming-edge alternative at any $t
otin\{r-1,r,r+1\}$, (c) at $t=r-1$, and (b) at $t=r+1$, while at $t=r$ both alternatives of step 3.1 fail because $r$ and $r+1$ lie in one row with $r$ to the left. A standard tableau with no incoming edge is $t^\mu$: if $T
e t^\mu$, choose the least $t$ with the node of $t+1$ earlier than the node of $t$ in $T$ (such $t$ exists because otherwise the entries occur in the order $1,2,\dots,d$); then standardness forces $t
earrow_Tt+1$ or an earlier component for $t+1$, so the incoming-edge alternative at $t$ holds and gives the existence of an edge into $T$, a contradiction. Hence in this final case $T=t^\mu$, which is alternative (4).

**The vertical terminal alternatives.** Let $\mu$ be a multipartition and $r\downarrow_Tr+1$ at $(a,b,n)$, so the two nodes are vertically adjacent. Use the following precise tests: (a) an incoming edge $t$ with $|t-r|>1$; (b) $r\nearrow_Tr+2$ or $r+1$ is in a later component than $r+2$; (c) $r-1\nearrow_Tr+1$ or $r-1$ is in a later component than $r$. Test (a) gives $s_tT\xrightarrow{t}T$ and preserves the vertical pair. In test (b), standardness and the consecutiveness of the three entries force $s_{r+1}T$ and $s_rs_{r+1}T$ to be standard: the node of $r+2$ is above and right of $r$, hence above and right of the node of $r+1$, and after the first swap the nodes of $r,r+1$ are incomparable. Thus $s_rs_{r+1}T\xrightarrow{r}s_{r+1}T\xrightarrow{r+1}T$, while $r+1,r+2$ occupy the original vertical pair in $s_rs_{r+1}T$. The different-component case uses the same two swaps without any within-component inequality. Test (c) gives the analogous $s_rs_{r-1}T\xrightarrow{r}s_{r-1}T\xrightarrow{r-1}T$, with $r-1,r$ in the original vertical pair. If none of the tests holds, labels other than the triple adjacent to $r$ cannot have an inversion between consecutive row-reading positions: any such inverse-order consecutive pair is in incomparable nodes or distinct components and is exactly an incoming edge. Reading $r-1,r-2,\ldots,1$ backwards and $r+2,r+3,\ldots,d$ forwards consequently places them in row-reading order except for the lower-row prefix before the vertical pair and the upper-row tail after it; tests (c) and (b) exclude any further excursion. More explicitly, if $L$ is the initial label at $(a,b,n)$ and $U$ the initial label at $(a+1,b,n)$, the forced belt filling is $L,\ldots,L+b-2$ in the first $b-1$ lower-row positions, $r=L+b-1$ in $(a,b,n)$, $r+1=L+b$ in $(a+1,b,n)$, and $L+b+1,\ldots,U$ in the remaining upper-row tail; all outside entries are unchanged. Among standard belt fillings this is Bruhat-maximal: the $b$ lower-row entries are the lexicographically smallest possible increasing subset, namely $L,\ldots,L+b-2,L+b$, because choosing the $b$ smallest would violate column $b$. Every other valid subset has no smaller prefix counts in the upper row, hence is below it by step 2.1. This is exactly the Garnir tableau, including $b=1=\mu_a$. A horizontal brick is a consecutive same-row string. All selections, chains and comparisons are finite, so no choice principle is used.

risk_review.notes: Read the entire Definition and eight proof steps plus all six exact dependency interfaces. BKW §3.2–3.4 pp.10–12 and the concluding Proposition 3.10 proof p.13 fix the left-action/strong-order orientation. Rank inequalities give the row-prefix iff in both directions; parabolic subwords confine the belt; the vertical prefix switch uses multipartition monotonicity; terminal swaps preserve standardness. The explicit maximal belt filling gives the unique standard maximum, including b=1=upper-row-length; rank zero has the empty tableau and no swap/belt obligation. citations.quote: Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over a field and let $J=J(A)$. Then $J$ is nilpotent, and the quotient algebra $A/J$ is semisimple.

Let $R$ be a nonzero unital ring. Then $R$ is semisimple if and only if $$R\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i)$$ for positive integers $r,n_i$ and division rings $D_i$. See [[thm-endomorphism-ring-of-the-left-regular-module-is-opposite]].

Let $r\ge1$, let every $n_i\ge1$, let every $D_i$ be a division ring, and put $R=\prod_{i=1}^rM_{n_i}(D_i)$. Then every simple left $R$-module is supported on exactly one factor and is isomorphic to that factor's column module $D_i^{n_i}$. These column modules give all simple left $R$-module isomorphism classes, with one class for each factor. See [[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]].
A nonzero homomorphism between simple modules is an isomorphism. Consequently the endomorphism ring of a simple module is a division ring. See [[def-simple-module]].

Let $p\in F[x]$ be monic and irreducible, and put $K=F[x]/(p)$ and $a=x+(p)$. Then $K$ is a field extension of $F$, $p(a)=0$, and every element of $K$ has a unique representative $r$ with $\deg r<\deg p$ (with $r=0$ allowed). In particular, if $\deg p=n$, every element is uniquely $$c_0+c_1a+\cdots+c_{n-1}a^{n-1},\qquad c_j\in F.$$

The orbit $A_{\mathbb Z}v_{\mathbb Q}$ is generated as an abelian group by the images of a finite integer basis of $A_{\mathbb Z}$. It is torsion-free because it is a subgroup of a rational vector space. Its rational span is $D_{\mathbb Q}$, by cyclicity, so its rank equals $\dim_{\mathbb Q}D_{\mathbb Q}=\dim_KD_K$. derivations.claim: Let M be a nonzero finite-dimensional standard homogeneous cyclotomic module. Choose a nonzero word by successively maximizing the last constant-color block, then the preceding block after restricting that maximum, until the vacuum is reached. Write the resulting word as i_1^{r_1}...i_s^{r_s}, adjacent colors distinct. Restriction to a word idempotent is exact. Every simple constituent of M with nonzero word space must have precisely the same first maximal last-block length: a shorter length gives zero, a longer length would contradict maximality for M. The actual maximal-tail supplier identifies the full maximal restriction of this simple with N tensor L(i_s^{r_s}), where N is simple with zero residual i_s-tail. Repeat on N and on the corresponding exact restriction of M. At the end N is the unique vacuum simple. Reconstruct using the actual unique-head induction supplier. Hence exactly one simple shift orbit among the constituents of M can contribute at the chosen word. Its crystal label is obtained by the same successive right-induction powers from the vacuum, so is field independent under the native11 canonical B(Lambda) identification.

For the normalized simple S in that orbit, maximal restriction is normalized N tensor normalized L(i^r): restriction commutes with finite vector duality, the two factors are absolutely simple, and their unique self-dual normalizations force the remaining shift to be zero. The normalized rank-r nil-Hecke simple has graded dimension [r]_i!, by the actual polynomial/corner calculation with shift -d_i binomial(r,2). Iterating gives gdim e(word)S=product_a [r_a]_{i_a}!. Therefore the coefficient of [S] in [M] is gdim e(word)M divided by this nonzero product.

For character injectivity, realize the finite set of simple orbits appearing in a virtual relation as their direct sum, choose an extremal word as above, and evaluate the relation: exactly one orbit contributes, with its nonzero factorial polynomial. Its Laurent coefficient is zero. Remove it and repeat on the remaining finite set. This proves injectivity without assuming the relation is a module.

Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine
Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple
roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and
$\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and
the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is
the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the
English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime
$p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two
classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

**The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and
$i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of
residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the list in reverse order, with the opposite cancellation, and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

**The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let
$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ of
[[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on
*all* partitions). When the wedge bar $\psi$ is supplied by the global-basis
construction, transport it by the formula below; this convention does not
construct that bar. The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

**Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$
exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by
$D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently
$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);
for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

Let $F:=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathbb Q(q)|\lambda\rangle$ be the charge-$0$ part of
the Fock space of
[[lem-semi-infinite-wedges-are-indexed-by-partitions-and-give-node-action-formulas]],
with basis indexed by all partitions and with the node operators $F_i,E_i$
defined by the stable finite-prefix action. Assign to $|\lambda\rangle$ the
**level-one weight**

$$\mathrm{wt}(|\lambda\rangle):=\Lambda_0-\sum_{i\in I}m_i(\lambda)\,\alpha_i, \qquad m_i(\lambda):=\#\{\text{cells of }\lambda\text{ of residue }i\},$$

where the **residue** of a cell in row $r$ and column $c$ is $c-r\bmod e$, and
the **size** $|\lambda|$ is the separate grading. The vacuum is the empty
partition $\varnothing$; $F_i$ adds and $E_i$ removes a node by the explicit
finite node formulas of the same item. The toral action is
$K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$ with $N_i$ the
addable-minus-removable count, proved to be the Cartan pairing in
[[lem-the-node-count-is-the-level-one-cartan-pairing]], and
$K_d|\lambda\rangle=q^{-m_0(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$.

A partition is **$e$-regular** if each positive part occurs with multiplicity
$<e$, and **$e$-restricted** if $\lambda_r-\lambda_{r+1}<e$ for every $r\ge1$
(with $\lambda_{r}=0$ beyond the length). These operators are declared linear
endomorphisms here; the affine relations proved later establish the actual
module structure, so nothing about $F$ is silently assumed in this Definition.

The constructed node operators on **all** partition vectors make the charge-$0$
partition Fock space $F$ into a $P$-graded integrable module for
$U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_e)$ with the fixed coproduct and the cyclic Cartan
datum: all toral commutation rules and mixed commutators
$[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ hold, and both quantum Serre
sums vanish, including the cubic $e=2$ case with
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ and $[3]=q^2+1+q^{-2}$. Each color acts on finite Boolean
cubes, and $F_i,E_i$ change the $P$-weight by $\mp\alpha_i$. Ordinary standard
coefficients may have $q^{-1}$ poles; normalized Kashiwara lattice stability is
a separate statement.

Work in the linear symmetric-group model of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]]: the
$\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism $J M_\mu = |\mu'\rangle$, the transported
action, bar and $A_0$ standard chart $(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$, and the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\mu) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\mu)\alpha_i$, with
$A = \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$.

**The basic module and its lower basis.** Let
$M_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1}V(\Lambda_0) = J^{-1}M_{\mathrm{QG}}$ be the
transported highest-weight module of the vacuum; by
[[thm-restricted-partition-component-is-the-basic-crystal-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]]
its crystal is the $e$-restricted component and its labels are the $e$-restricted
partitions. For an $e$-restricted $\lambda$ define
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) := J^{-1}G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\lambda'),$$
where $G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\mu)$ is the lower global (canonical) basis element of
the Fock space at the standard vector $|\mu\rangle$
([[thm-the-basic-representation-global-basis-is-unitriangular-in-the-partition-basis]]).
Then $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) \equiv M_\lambda \bmod q\,(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$
and the family $\{G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)\}$ is the transported lower global
basis of $M_{\mathrm{sym}}$, indexed by the restricted labels. Define the
**level-one transition polynomials in the symmetric-group convention** by the
finite weightwise expansion
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) = \sum_\mu d_{(\lambda,\mu)}(q)\, M_\mu ,$$
the sum being over the partitions $\mu$ of the weight of $\lambda$.

**Ambient polarization and ambient upper coordinates.** Define the ambient
polarization by $B(M_\mu,M_\nu) = \delta_{\mu\nu}$ on the standard basis, a
symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form on each finite weight space. Fix a weight
$w$ and let $V_w$ be the (finite-dimensional) weight space of
$F_{\mathrm{sym}}$; let $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ be the matrix with columns the
coordinate vectors of $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)$ for the finitely many
$e$-restricted $\lambda$ of weight $w$, and rows the **standard** shapes
$M_\mu$, $\mu$ of weight $w$; let
$$H := D_{\mathrm{rect}}^{\mathsf{t}}\, D_{\mathrm{rect}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda) := \sum_\mu \bigl(D_{\mathrm{rect}}H^{-1}\bigr)_{(\mu,\lambda)}\, M_\mu^* ,$$
where $M_\mu^*$ denotes the ambient orthonormal dual frame of the standard
basis. The $G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda)$ are the **ambient upper coordinates**
of the basic module: they are the unique elements of the basic subspace
$(M_{\mathrm{sym}})_w\subseteq V_w$ characterized weightwise by $B(G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda), G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda')) = \delta_{\lambda\lambda'}$,
and are viewed in the ambient standard frame; adding a vector of the
$B$-orthogonal complement in $V_w$ gives other ambient representatives with
the same pairings. The coefficients
$e_{(\lambda,\mu)}(q) := (D_{\mathrm{rect}}H^{-1})_{(\mu,\lambda)}$ lie in
$\mathbb{Q}(q)$ but need not be Laurent integral or polynomial. They are
coordinates in the ambient space and not a "standard basis of the basic
module"; the exact integral upper basis is the transported upper global basis of
[[thm-upper-and-lower-global-bases-are-dual-and-crystal-compatible]], whose
restricted graded $A$-dual lattice is free weightwise and perfectly paired with
the basic lower $A$-span, while no lower-$A$ selfduality, no $A$-unit $H$ and no
full algebraic duality in infinite rank is implied. The restriction of $B$ to the basic module equals the normalized transported
contravariant form (proved in step 4.2), so these are the same upper vectors
viewed in the ambient standard frame and in their own integral dual lattice.
Upper bar is the adjoint bar
$\psi^\vee$ with its own dual infinity chart and weighted upper operators, not
the ordinary lower bar.

**The full ambient case.** On the whole Fock space the analogous matrix
$D_{\mathrm{full}}$, with columns the $G(\mu)$ over all partitions and rows the
standard shapes, is unitriangular (diagonal $1$, in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$ below the
diagonal), and the dual matrix with respect to $B$ is
$$D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}},$$
which is Laurent integral because the inverse of a unitriangular matrix with
entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$ has entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$.

**A worked instance.** At $e = 2$ the restricted shape $\lambda = (1,1)$ has
$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(1,1) = M_{1,1} + q\,M_{2}$, so $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ has the
single column $(q,1)^{\mathsf{t}}$, $H = 1 + q^2$, and
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(1,1) = \frac{M_{1,1}^* + q\,M_2^*}{1+q^2} = \frac{M_{1,1} + q\,M_2}{1+q^2},$$
an explicit ambient coordinate that is rational but not Laurent integral:
$1 + q^2$ is not a unit of $\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$. No specialization of the $d$
to decomposition numbers of Hecke algebras is asserted here without the
separate correct Hecke parameter hypotheses.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Fix an integer $e\ge 2$ and put $I:=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z=\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$
with its cyclic order; elements of $I$ are called **residues**. Let
$A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ be the integer matrix with

$$a_{ii}=2,\qquad a_{i,i-1}=a_{i,i+1}=-1\ \ (i\in I)$$

when $e\ge 3$, and with $a_{00}=a_{11}=2$ and the single double edge
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ when $e=2$; all indices are read modulo $e$. Thus for
$e\ge3$ all off-diagonal entries other than the neighbouring entries $-1$ are
$0$, and for $e=2$ the matrix is
$\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$. Take the diagonal symmetrizer
$D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\dots,1)$ and the quantum parameter $q$ over
$\mathbb Q$, so that $q_i=q^{d_i}=q$ for every $i\in I$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]).

Choose free abelian groups

$$P=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\Lambda_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z\delta, \qquad P^{\vee}=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z h_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z d,$$

with the $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times
P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$ determined by

$$\langle\Lambda_j,h_i\rangle=\delta_{ij},\qquad \langle\delta,h_i\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\Lambda_j,d\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\delta,d\rangle=1 .$$

For $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $\lambda\in P$, also use the transposed notation
$\langle h,\lambda\rangle:=\langle\lambda,h\rangle$. This notation pairs
a coweight with a weight and is distinct from the symmetric weight form below.

Define the **simple roots**

$$\alpha_i:=\sum_{j\in I}a_{ji}\Lambda_j+\delta_{i0}\,\delta\qquad(i\in I),$$

let $Q:=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\alpha_i\subseteq P$ be the **root lattice**
and $Q^+$ its nonnegative cone, and define the **central element**
$c:=\sum_{i\in I}h_i\in P^{\vee}$. The **level** of $\lambda\in P$ is
$\langle c,\lambda\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ ([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]),
and the **classical weight lattice** is $P_{\mathrm{cl}}:=P/\mathbb Z\delta$.

The **diagram reflection** $\tau$ is the pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear
involutions $\tau:P\to P$, $P^{\vee}\to P^{\vee}$ with
$\tau(\Lambda_i)=\Lambda_{-i}$, $\tau(\delta)=\delta$, $\tau(h_i)=h_{-i}$ and
$\tau(d)=d$ (indices negated in $\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$).

The **normalized affine weight form** is the symmetric $\mathbb Q$-bilinear form on $P_{\mathbb Q}:=P\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ determined, in the decomposition $P_{\mathbb Q}=Q_{\mathbb Q}\oplus\mathbb Q\Lambda_0$, by

$$(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)=a_{ij},\qquad (\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)=\delta_{i0},\qquad (\Lambda_0,\Lambda_0)=0.$$

Thus, for $x=\sum_i x_i\alpha_i$, $y=\sum_i y_i\alpha_i$ and $t,s\in\mathbb Q$, set

$$(x+t\Lambda_0,y+s\Lambda_0)=\sum_{i,j}x_i a_{ij}y_j+t y_0+s x_0.$$

In particular $(\lambda,\alpha_i)=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle$ and $(\lambda,\delta)=\langle\lambda,c\rangle$. Its restriction to $Q$ is integer-valued; on all of $P$ it is rational-valued. This form on weights is distinct from the weight-coweight pairing. Define $s_i(\lambda):=\lambda-\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\alpha_i$ and let $W$ be the group generated by these simple reflections; the form is $W$-invariant and $\tau$-invariant.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum with finite color set $I$ and no imaginary
simple roots, a KLR datum $Q=(Q_{ij})_{i\ne j}$ satisfying (Q1)-(Q4), and a
field $k$ placed in degree zero
([[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]],
[[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]); let
$R=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q_+}R(\beta)$ be the resulting graded KLR algebra, with
its idempotents $e(\nu)$, dots $x_a$, crossings $\tau_a$ and degrees
$\deg x_a=2d_{\nu_a}$, $\deg\tau_a=-b_{\nu_a\nu_{a+1}}$
([[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]]). Let $\Lambda$ be a
dominant integral weight and put $\lambda_i:=\langle h_i,\Lambda\rangle\ge0$
([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]).

**Cyclotomic data.** For every color $i$ choose a monic polynomial
$a_i(u)\in k[u]$ of degree exactly $\lambda_i$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]); the standard choice made
below is $a_i(u)=u^{\lambda_i}$. For $n\ge1$ write
$$a(x_s)=\sum_{\nu\in I^n}a_{\nu_s}(x_s)e(\nu)\qquad(1\le s\le n),$$
the element of $R_n(Q)$ that acts on the $\nu$-component by the monic
polynomial $a_{\nu_s}$ in the dot at position $s$.

**The cyclotomic quotient.** For $\beta\in Q_+$ define $J_a(\beta)$ to be the
two-sided ideal of $R(\beta)$ generated by the first-strand elements
$a_{\nu_1}(x_1)e(\nu)$, $\nu\in I^\beta$; equivalently
$$J_a(\beta)=\sum_{\nu\in I^\beta}R(\beta)\,a_{\nu_1}(x_1)e(\nu)\,R(\beta),$$
and put
$$R_a^\Lambda(\beta):=R(\beta)/J_a(\beta),\qquad R_a^\Lambda(0):=k .$$
The **cyclotomic KLR algebra** is the direct sum
$R_a^\Lambda:=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q_+}R_a^\Lambda(\beta)$; it carries the
local units $e(\beta)=\sum_{\nu\in I^\beta}e(\nu)$, which act as the identity
on $R_a^\Lambda(\beta)$ and annihilate the other summands, and it is a
$k$-algebra with these orthogonal idempotents.

**Standard choice and grading.** The STANDARD choice $a_i(u)=u^{\lambda_i}$ is
used throughout the graded categorification, duality-normalization and based
statements below; for it we write $R^\Lambda:=R^\Lambda_a$. Under the standard
choice each individual first-strand generator
$x_1^{\lambda_{\nu_1}}e(\nu)$ is homogeneous of degree
$2d_{\nu_1}\lambda_{\nu_1}$ in the grading of
[[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]], so the ideal $J_a(\beta)$
and the quotient $R^\Lambda(\beta)$ are graded, and $R^\Lambda$ is a
$\mathbb Z$-graded algebra with local units. The sum $a(x_1)$ itself need not
have one common degree across different colors, and no single degree is
assigned to it.

**Boundary of the definition.** Arbitrary monic polynomials with lower
coefficients in degree-zero $k$ give an UNGRADED deformation $R_a^\Lambda$;
nilpotent dots, homogeneous trace degree and the highest-weight graded $K_0$
identification are not asserted for that branch, and the ungraded branch is
used only where a statement explicitly says so. Finite dimension, finite root
strings, ordinary projectivity and symmetry of the standard quotient have the
separately stated monic conclusions below. The cyclotomic relation is imposed
on the FIRST strand, and cyclotomic induction appends strands on the RIGHT
([[def-cyclotomic-klr-induction-and-restriction-functors]]); this convention
fixes the side on which the quotient map acts throughout the page.

This definition uses no choice.

Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine
Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple
roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and
$\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and
the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is
the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the
English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime
$p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two
classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

**The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and
$i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of
residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the list in reverse order, with the opposite cancellation, and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

**The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let
$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ of
[[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on
*all* partitions). When the wedge bar $\psi$ is supplied by the global-basis
construction, transport it by the formula below; this convention does not
construct that bar. The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

**Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$
exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by
$D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently
$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);
for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: **The level-one cyclotomic relation.** By [F2], $(\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)=\delta_{i,0}$, so the cyclotomic polynomial of the level-one Hecke presentation is $\prod_i(X_1-\xi^i)^{(\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)}=X_1-1$ and the KLR first-strand cyclotomic relation is $y_1^{\delta_{i,0}}e(i)=0$ [F2, F3]. Consequently the level-one Hecke quotient is the finite type-$A$ Hecke algebra with $T_r^2=(\xi-1)T_r+\xi$ and its residue-content blocks are the $e_\alpha H^\Lambda_d$, as stated by the level-one finite-Hecke supplier [F6].

**The two sub-branches.** By [F1] the given $\xi\ne1$ has multiplicative order $e$. In characteristic $p>0$, if $p\mid e$, then $X^e-1=(X^{e/p}-1)^p$ implies $\xi^{e/p}=1$, contradicting this order. Thus $p\nmid e$ follows from the stated parameter hypothesis. In characteristic zero no such restriction is needed; both branches use the primitive root already given in $F$.

**Grading and transport conventions.** The KLR degrees are $\deg e(i)=0$, $\deg y_r=2$ and $\deg\psi_re(i)=-a_{i_ri_{r+1}}$ in the type-$A$ specialization with all $d_i=1$ [F3]. Transporting along the blockwise KLR isomorphism and an admissible local normalising series gives each Hecke block a $\mathbb Z$-grading, nontrivial on the corollary's level-one $e=2$ rank-two sector and trivial on a one-dimensional block, and two admissible series differ by the graded automorphism $\rho'\rho^{-1}$, so all graded multiplicities below are independent of the choice [F6].

**The Fock conventions.** The symmetric model has charge $0$, residues $c-r$, standard vectors indexed by all partitions, restricted labels the $e$-restricted partitions $RP_\alpha$, and empty component $B(\Lambda_0)$; the conjugate of a restricted partition is $e$-regular [F4]. These are exactly the labels used by the global basis expansions of the page.

**The theta dictionary and content reflection.** The sign automorphism satisfies $\theta(T_r)=(\xi-1)-T_r=-\xi T_r^{-1}$ and is an involution [F5]. On the finite level-one tower the Jucys--Murphy elements are the palindromic words $X_j=\xi^{1-j}T_{j-1}\cdots T_1T_1\cdots T_{j-1}$; applying $\theta$ to this palindrome inverts the generators in reversed order, which reproduces the same palindrome inverted, and the $2j-2$ factors contribute $(-\xi)^{2j-2}=\xi^{2j-2}$, so $\theta(X_j)=X_j^{-1}$ exactly, the scalar $1$ being the product of the displayed factors [F5]. On a generalized eigenvector with $X_jv=\xi^iv$ one therefore has $X_j^{-1}v=\xi^{-i}v$, so pulling back along the involution $\theta$ reflects every residue $i$ to $-\xi$-power $i\mapsto-i$ and hence sends charge-zero content $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$; the ordinary module carries the conjugate content before pullback and is not identified untwisted in the same block [F5, F6].

**The ungraded convention dictionary and no choice.** After converting right modules to left modules through the star anti-involution, the intrinsic restricted Murphy simple with label $\lambda$ is the $\theta$-pullback of $D_{\rm DJ}^{\lambda'}$, by the ordinary Specht-form comparison of [F6]; the Laurent-unit form factor of that comparison preserves radicals, so it includes the zero-quotient case and the dictionary is stable under applying the involution twice [F6]. The parameter $\xi$ of the Hecke algebra and the grading variable $q$ are kept independent, and no numerical relation between them is imposed. Every clause of the definition is a convention or a finite computation, so no choice principle is used.

citations.quote: If $A$ is also $\mathbb Z$-graded and $P,M$ are finite-dimensional graded left $A$-modules with $P$ projective in $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$, the generator value $h_{\mathrm{gr}}(P,M):=\sum_{d\in\mathbb Z}v^d\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,M)$ extends uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing $\langle-,-\rangle_{\mathrm{gr}}:K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)\times G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)\to R$, where $R:=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$.
These are candidate values on object isomorphism classes; no descent to pairings on $K_0\times G_0$ is asserted here.

Fix a graded $k$-algebra $A$ and let $P$ be a graded left $A$-module ([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). The category $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$ of graded left $A$-modules and degree-zero maps is abelian ([[lem-graded-module-kernels-cokernels-and-biproducts-are-degreewise]]). **Graded projective.** $P$ is **graded projective** when it is a projective object of $\operatorname

Let $k$ be a field and let $R=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_+}R_\alpha$ be a tower of
finite-dimensional unital $\mathbb Z$-graded $k$-algebras with local units
$e(\alpha)$: every finite root-supported element has a unit given by the sum of its finitely many sector units, each
$R_\alpha$ a direct summand and $R_0=k$. Define
$$K_0^{\rm gr}(R):=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_+}K_0^{\rm gr}(R_\alpha),\qquad G_0^{\rm gr}(R):=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_+}G_0^{\rm gr}(R_\alpha),$$
the restricted direct sums of the blockwise Grothendieck groups of
[[def-graded-grothendieck-group-shift-module-and-cartan-map]]:
$K_0^{\rm gr}(R_\alpha)$ of finitely generated graded left
$R_\alpha$-projectives modulo split exact sequences
([[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]]) and
$G_0^{\rm gr}(R_\alpha)$ of finite-dimensional graded left $R_\alpha$-modules
modulo short exact sequences. Both are modules over
$A:=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ by $q[M]:=[M\{1\}]$
([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]), and inside each
finite-dimensional block the shift-orbit bases of
[[thm-graded-projective-and-simple-classes-have-shift-orbit-bases]] hold. The
Cartan homomorphism $c:K_0^{\rm gr}(R)\to G_0^{\rm gr}(R)$, $[P]\mapsto[P]$, is
$A$-linear. The forgetful maps $\zeta$ to the ungraded groups $K_0(R)$,
$G_0(R)$ are additive and satisfy $\zeta(qm)=\zeta(m)$. The groups $K_0^{\rm gr}$ and
$G_0^{\rm gr}$ are DIFFERENT objects and are never identified.

**The two towers used below.** (i) For the standard homogeneous cyclotomic
quotient of [[def-cyclotomic-klr-quotient-at-a-dominant-weight]] at the
level-one weight $\Lambda_0$ of
[[def-type-a-cyclotomic-specialization-of-the-qg-klr-algebras]], put
$R^\Lambda_\alpha=R^\Lambda(\alpha)$; every block is finite dimensional and has
the homogeneous symmetrizing functional of
`thm-cyclotomic-klr-algebras-are-finite-dimensional-graded-symmetric`, with
grading shifts as in [[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]]. (ii) For
the cyclotomic Hecke tower $H^{\Lambda}:=\bigoplus_\alpha H^\Lambda_\alpha$ of
`def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras` with the block decomposition
of `def-residue-sequence-idempotents-and-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks`, fix an
admissible local normalising series and transport the homogeneous KLR
decomposition through the blockwise isomorphism of
`thm-brundan-kleshchev-blockwise-hecke-klr-isomorphism`, as in
`cor-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks-inherit-a-nontrivial-z-grading`; the induced
transport identifies $K_0^{\rm gr}(H^{\Lambda})\cong K_0^{\rm gr}(R^\Lambda)$
as $A$-modules and similarly for $G_0^{\rm gr}$, compatibly with $\zeta$ and
with the Cartan homomorphisms. Every class has finite root support, so the
direct sums are restricted.

No choice principle is used in this definition.

derivations.claim: **The pairing is defined and finite.** Fix a root degree $\alpha$. Since $R^\Lambda_\alpha$ is finite dimensional, a finite homogeneous generating family makes $P$ a quotient of a finite sum of shifted regular modules, hence finite dimensional. Each $\operatorname{Hom}_{R^\Lambda_\alpha,d}(P,M)$ is a subspace of the finite-dimensional space of $k$-linear maps from $P$ to $M$. The finite grading supports of $P$ and $M$ imply that this subspace vanishes unless $d\in\operatorname{supp}(M)-\operatorname{supp}(P)$. Thus the sum defining $h_\alpha(P,M)$ is a finite Laurent polynomial, including zero when either module is zero.

**The pairing descends.** Additivity of the graded Hom pairing in $P$ and $M$, and its behaviour under split exact sequences in $P$ and short exact sequences in $M$, are those of [F1]; therefore $h_\alpha$ descends to $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(R^\Lambda_\alpha)\times G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(R^\Lambda_\alpha)$ and, by the restricted-support definition of the towers, to the displayed pairing on the restricted direct sums [F1].

**The twist formula.** Internal shift satisfies $\operatorname{Hom}_d(P\{r\},M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{d+r}(P,M)$, so $h_\alpha(P\{r\},M)=q^{-r}h_\alpha(P,M)$ and $h_\alpha(P,M\{s\})=q^{s}h_\alpha(P,M)$; hence $h(q^r[P],q^s[M])=q^{s-r}h([P],[M])$, the sesquilinear twist of [F1] [F1]. In particular $h^0(P,S)=\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}^0(P,S)$ is the coefficient of $q^0$ in $h(P,S)$; evaluation at $q=1$ instead sums the dimensions in all degrees.

**Transport and duality conventions.** The transport isomorphisms of [F3] identify the Hecke-side groups with the KLR-side groups and carry internal shift to internal shift, so the pairing defined above transports to the Hecke side without change; the dualities $\psi$, $D_\psi$ and $\#$ are shift-reversing involutions of [F3], and each graded-simple shift orbit has the unique $D_\psi$-self-dual representative of [F3], and its indecomposable projective cover has the normalized $\#$-self-dual grading with $\operatorname{Hom}^0(P,S)=k$. These assertions concern simples and their indecomposable covers; they do not normalize every projective direct sum by an overall shift [F3]. No perfectness, nondegeneracy or $A$-self-duality is asserted at this point; those are the content of the integral highest weight identification named in the Definition.

**No choice.** Every ingredient is a finite-dimensional block, a finite Laurent polynomial or a transported isomorphism; the normalized representatives are selected canonically inside their orbits by the duality fixing condition, and no family of nonempty sets is selected. Hence no choice principle is used.
