citations.quote:
**Parameters.** Let $F$ be a field and $\xi\in F^\times$ with finite quantum
characteristic $e=e(F,\xi)\in\{2,3,\dots\}$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). We work in
the NONDEGENERATE branch $\xi\ne1$; then $\xi$ is a primitive $e$-th root of
unity in $F$, and all statements on this page live in one of the two
sub-branches: (C0) $\operatorname{char}F=0$, or (CP)
$\operatorname{char}F=p>0$ with $p\nmid e$. The Hecke parameter is written
$\xi$ here; it is the letter $q$ of `def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras`.

**Hecke side.** Fix the level-one fundamental weight $\Lambda_0$ of the cyclic
affine type-$A$ datum with all $d_i=1$ and charge $0$
([[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]). With the conventions of
`def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras`, $H^\Lambda_d=H_{F,\xi}(S_d)$
is the finite type-$A$ Hecke algebra $T_r^2=(\xi-1)T_r+\xi$
(`prop-cyclotomic-hecke-algebras-of-level-one-are-finite-hecke-algebras`), and
$H^\Lambda_\alpha=e_\alpha H^\Lambda_d$ are its residue-content blocks
(`def-residue-sequence-idempotents-and-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks`).

**KLR side.** Use the type-$A$ specialization $Q^A$ of
`def-type-a-cyclotomic-specialization-of-the-qg-klr-algebras` with the same $e$
and the STANDARD homogeneous first-strand cyclotomic quotient
$R^\Lambda_\alpha$ of [[def-cyclotomic-klr-quotient-at-a-dominant-weight]]: the
cyclotomic relation is $y_1^{\delta_{i_1,0}}e(i)=0$, induction appends on the
right, and the grading is $\deg e(i)=0$, $\deg y_r=2$,
$\deg\psi_re(i)=-a_{i_ri_{r+1}}$
([[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]]). The transported grading on
$H^\Lambda_\alpha$ uses a FIXED admissible local normalising series
(`cor-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks-inherit-a-nontrivial-z-grading`); a different
series gives a graded-isomorphic transported algebra via $\rho'\rho^{-1}$, and
the graded multiplicities studied below do not depend on the choice.

**Grading and Fock variables.** All grading shifts and all global-basis
polynomials are in the variable $q$, $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. Thus
$\xi\in F^\times$ (the Hecke parameter) and $q$ (the grading variable) are
INDEPENDENT data; the phrase "Ariki's normalization $\xi=q^2$" is retained only
as the source dictionary of [Ariki 1996], whose Hecke parameters are powers of
a square, and no numerical relation or specialization between $\xi$ and $q$ is
imposed.

**Fock side.** Use the level-one symmetric model of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]]: charge
$0$, node residues $c-r$, standard vectors $M_\mu$ for ALL partitions $\mu$,
basic/restricted labels the $e$-restricted partitions
$RP_\alpha=\{\lambda:\lambda_a-\lambda_{a+1}<e,\ \operatorname{cont}(\lambda)=\alpha\}$,
empty component $B(\Lambda_0)$. For $\lambda\in RP$ the conjugate $\lambda'$ is
$e$-regular. Write $P(\nu)$ for the independently constructed ordinary
Dipper--James Specht module and $D_{\rm DJ}^{\nu}$ for its form quotient in
`thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell`. Define
$\theta(T_r)=(\xi-1)-T_r=-\xi T_r^{-1}$, the involutive sign automorphism of
[[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. After converting right
modules to left modules through the star anti-involution, the intrinsic
restricted Murphy simple with label $\lambda$ is the $\theta$-pullback of
$D_{\rm DJ}^{\lambda'}$, not the untwisted ordinary module. This is an ungraded
convention dictionary. The pullback can move blocks: on the multiplicative
Jucys--Murphy elements $\theta(X_j)=X_j^{-1}$, so charge-zero residue content
is sent from $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$. Thus the ordinary module before pullback has
the conjugate content; no claim identifies it untwisted inside the same block.
At $\xi=1$ the separate specialization theorem
`cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary`
identifies $\theta$ with sign tensoring over every field; $\xi=1$ remains
outside the present nondegenerate regime.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge0$ and $\ell\ge1$, and let $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$
be units of $R$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). The **arbitrary-level
cyclotomic Hecke algebra** $H_n=H_n(R;z;U_1,\dots,U_\ell)$ is the $R$-algebra
presented by invertible commuting elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ subject to the relations
$$(T_i-z)(T_i+1)=0,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$
$$T_iX_iT_i=zX_{i+1},\qquad X_jT_i=T_iX_j\quad(j\notin\{i,i+1\}),\qquad \prod_{a=1}^{\ell}(X_1-U_a)=0 .$$
For $n=0$ set $H_0=R$. The **grading variable** of this page is $v$, not the
unit $z$: the two are identified only where a statement says so explicitly.

**Multipartitions and Murphy data.** An $\ell$-**multipartition** of $n$ is an
ordered tuple $\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(\ell)})$ of partitions
with $\sum_{b}|\lambda^{(b)}|=n$ ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).
Multipartitions are partially ordered by dominance, $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ meaning
that $\sum_{b<k}|\lambda^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\lambda^{(k)}_j\ge
\sum_{b<k}|\mu^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\mu^{(k)}_j$ for all $k,m$. Fill the
diagram $t^\lambda$ with $1,\dots,n$ in component order, then row order, then
column order. Put $a_k:=\sum_{b<k}|\lambda^{(b)}|$,
$u_\lambda:=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell}\prod_{j\le a_k}(X_j-U_k)$,
$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, and $m_\lambda:=x_\lambda u_\lambda$,
where $S_\lambda$ is the row subgroup: the subgroup of $S_n$ stabilizing the
rows of $t^\lambda$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $M_\lambda:=m_\lambda H_n$ for
the right $H_n$-submodule generated by $m_\lambda$
([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). The **presentation involution** $*$ of $H_n$
fixes every $X_j$ and every $T_i$ and reverses products. For standard
tableaux $s,t$ of shape $\lambda$ put $m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$,
where the right tableau action is $t\cdot w:=w^{-1}\cdot t$ (the left action relabels entries), and $d(s)$ is determined by $t^\lambda\cdot d(s)=s$.
Denote by $H^{>\lambda}$ the span of the higher Murphy shapes once their
basis and cell law is established by
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]], and by
$S_\lambda$ the right cell (**Specht**) module with basis $m_t$ and the
action given by that cell law; its cellular form defines
$D_\lambda:=S_\lambda/\operatorname{rad}S_\lambda$, which may vanish.

**Types.** The types used below are **exactly** all $\ell$-multipartitions of
$n$, including tuples with empty components — not all multicompositions. A
**semistandard tableau** $S$ has entries the labels $(i,k)$ (row $i$ in
component $k$) ordered by component first and then by row, weakly increasing
along rows, strictly increasing down columns, and a label of component $a$
may occur only in physical component $b\le a$
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]); the **type** of $S$ is the
multipartition counting each label with the multiplicity of the corresponding
row. For standard $s$ let $\mu(s)$ be the tableau obtained from $s$ by
replacing each entry by its row-and-component in $t^{\mu}$. Put
$$m_{(S,t)}:=\sum_{s:\,\mu(s)=S}m_{st},\qquad m_{(S,T)}:=\sum_{s,t:\,\mu(s)=S,\ \nu(t)=T}m_{st}.$$
Let
$$M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda\ \text{multipartition of}\ n}M_\lambda,\qquad C_n:=\operatorname{End}_{H_n}(M),$$
with ordinary composition ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]). For
$S,T$ of shape $\lambda$ and types $\mu,\nu$, the map $\varphi_{ST}$ — once
justified by [[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] —
sends $m_\alpha h$ to $\delta_{\alpha,\nu}m_{(S,T)}h$. Its right cell module
$\Delta_\lambda$ has basis $v_T$ over the semistandard $T$ of multipartition
types, with contravariant cell form and quotient $L_\lambda$. Let $T^\lambda$
be the unique tableau of shape and type $\lambda$, and let $e_\lambda$ be the
identity projection onto $M_\lambda$. Put $\omega:=(\varnothing,\dots,\varnothing,(1^n))$
and $e:=e_\omega$; then $m_\omega=1$, so $M_\omega=H_n$, and $H_n$ is an
actual direct summand of $M$. The weight projections used by the Jantzen
theory below are the $e_\nu$ with $\nu$ a multipartition. Write
$K_{(\lambda,\nu)}:=\#\operatorname{SStd}_\nu(\lambda)$ for the number of
semistandard tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and type $\nu$.

**Boundary of the definition.** All asserted module, form and map laws are
discharged by the linked local suppliers
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]],
[[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] and
[[thm-cyclotomic-schur-standards-and-schur-functor-control-block-linkage]];
the definition itself claims no proof of them and no primitive
residue-content classification. No choice principle is used: only finite
bases, finite subgroup and coset decompositions, finite filtrations and
explicit polynomial identities occur.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $[\lambda]$ be its Young diagram
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A **tableau of shape
$\lambda$**, or $\lambda$-tableau, is a bijection
$$t:[\lambda]\longrightarrow\{1,2,\dots,n\}.$$
We write $t(i,j)$ for the entry of $t$ in the node $(i,j)$, and we display $t$
as the diagram $[\lambda]$ with each node carrying its entry. Thus a tableau
places each of the numbers $1,\dots,n$ in exactly one node of $[\lambda]$. For
$\lambda=\varnothing$ the diagram is empty and the empty map is the unique
tableau of shape $\varnothing$, the **empty tableau**. The **shape** of a
tableau $t$ is the partition $\lambda$ with $t:[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$,
which is determined by $t$ because $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$.

**Standard tableaux.** A tableau $t$ of shape $\lambda$ is **standard** if its
entries strictly increase along rows and down columns, that is, if
$$t(i,j)<t(i,j+1)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i,j+1)\in[\lambda],$$
$$t(i,j)<t(i+1,j)\quad\text{whenever }(i,j),(i+1,j)\in[\lambda].$$
The empty tableau is standard, because both conditions are vacuous, and it is
the unique standard tableau of shape $\varnothing$. Following the classical
notation we write $f^\lambda$ for the number of standard $\lambda$-tableaux.

**The left action on tableaux.** For $\sigma\in S_n$ and a $\lambda$-tableau
$t$, define
$$(\sigma\cdot t)(i,j):=\sigma\bigl(t(i,j)\bigr)\qquad\bigl((i,j)\in[\lambda]\bigr).$$
Since $t$ is a bijection onto $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $\sigma$ is a bijection of
$\{1,\dots,n\}$, the map $\sigma\cdot t$ is again a bijection
$[\lambda]\to\{1,\dots,n\}$, hence again a $\lambda$-tableau, and
$\mathrm{id}\cdot t=t$, $\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot t)=(\sigma\tau)\cdot t$ for all
$\sigma,\tau\in S_n$: the rule is a left action of $S_n$ on the set of
$\lambda$-tableaux. For every $\sigma\in S_n$ the row sets of $\sigma\cdot t$
are the images under $\sigma$ of the row sets of $t$, and the column sets of
$\sigma\cdot t$ are the images under $\sigma$ of the column sets of $t$.

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For $1\le k\le n$ define
$$L_1:=0,\qquad L_k:=q^{-1}T_{(k-1,k)}+q^{-2}T_{(k-2,k)}+\cdots+q^{1-k}T_{(1,k)}\in H\quad(k\ge2),$$
where $T_{(i,k)}$ is the standard basis element indexed by the transposition
$(i\ k)$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). The $L_k$
are the **Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements**. They are fixed by the star
anti-automorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$
([[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): each
transposition $(i\ k)$ is its own inverse, so $T_{(i,k)}^*=T_{(i,k)}$, and the
coefficients $q^{i-k}$ are central, whence
$L_k^*=\sum_{i<k}q^{i-k}T_{(i,k)}=L_k$. They commute pairwise and every
symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with coefficients in $R$ is central in
$H$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of
[[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to
negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that
$(q-1)[m]_q=q^m-1$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$. When $q-1$ is a unit this
may be written $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$; the polynomial definition requires no
such division. Also $[m]_1=m$ for all
$m\in\mathbb Z$, since $[-r]_1=-[r]_1=-r$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$
and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the
node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the
**q-content value** $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$. If $e=e(F,q)<\infty$ for
a field $F$ then $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), so the
q-content value depends only on the residue of the content modulo $e$. At $q=1$
the identification $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$ — the
isomorphism given by the Coxeter presentation and the standard bases
([[thm-the-symmetric-group-has-the-coxeter-presentation]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) — sends $L_k$ to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy element
$X_k=\sum_{j<k}(j\ k)$
([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), because each
coefficient $q^{j-k}$ specializes to $1$, and
$[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_1=\operatorname{content}_t(k)$.

derivations.claim: **The ideal and the cyclic generator.** The span $K(\mu)$ of the Murphy elements indexed by standard pairs of shape strictly dominating $\mu$ is a two-sided ideal by the cellularity theorem `thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular`, and the class $z_\mu=m_{t^\mu t^\mu}+K(\mu)$ is the canonical generator of the cell module [F2]. The left action is obtained from the right cellular datum by $h\cdot m=mh^*$, so $S(\mu)=H^\Lambda_dz_\mu$ is a left module; no right module is identified with a left module without this conversion [F2].

**The initial weight vector and block.** The row-filled tableau $t^\mu$ dominates every standard tableau of its shape at every prefix. Thus the triangular JM formula of [[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]] has no off-diagonal terms at this vector. Star fixes $L_r$, so conversion to the left cell module gives $L_rz_\mu=[c-r]_\xi z_\mu$ for the node $(r,c)$ containing that entry. The multiplicative JM recurrence $X_{a+1}=\xi^{-1}T_aX_aT_a$ and the quadratic relation give $X_a=1+(\xi-1)L_a$: its inductive step is $L_{a+1}=\xi^{-1}T_aL_aT_a+\xi^{-1}T_a$. Hence $X_az_\mu=\xi^{i_a}z_\mu$ by $1+(\xi-1)[m]_\xi=\xi^m$, valid also for negative content. The weight idempotents and $y_a=(1-\xi^{-i_a}X_a)e(i)$ now give $e(i_{t^\mu})z_\mu=z_\mu$ and $y_az_\mu=0$. Since the vectors generated from $z_\mu$ have sequences obtained by permuting its residues, the whole cyclic module lies in content block $\alpha=\operatorname{cont}(\mu)$.

**The vectors.** For each standard $\mu$-tableau $T$ fix a reduced decomposition $w_T=s_{r_1}\cdots s_{r_m}$; the elements $z_T=T_{w_T}z_\mu$ and $v_T=\psi_{w_T}z_\mu$ are defined by left multiplication in the Hecke and KLR presentations, and $T_{w_T}$ is independent of its Hecke reduced expression, whereas $\psi_{w_T}z_\mu$ can depend on the chosen reduced word: the KLR braid relation has correction terms [F5]. The resulting family is defined for the selected reduced words, and the discharge theorem proves that every selected family gives the same graded subspaces; it does not assert that the individual vectors are word-independent [F5].

**The degree recursion is well defined.** For a standard tableau $T$ of size $d>0$, $T_{\le d-1}$ is a standard tableau of the smaller shape and the node $A$ of $T$ containing $d$ is removable in that shape, so the recursion $\deg(T)=\deg(T_{\le d-1})+d_A(\mu)$ is a finite induction on $d$ with values in $\mathbb Z$ depending only on $T$ and $\mu$; the declared boundary count is evaluated in the same residue convention at every stage [F1, F3].

**The ungraded comparisons and Choice.** Forgetting the grading, the star-contragredient duality of `thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual` identifies the left cell module with the same-shape Specht dual, and the signed-conjugate comparison of `thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell` gives $S(\mu)\cong P(\mu')^{\theta}$ after conversion; since $\theta$ commutes with star by [F4], both comparisons keep their stated positions and neither asserts untwisted conjugate identification [F4]. Every construction selects finite sets of reduced decompositions and finite basis data, so no choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
**Parameters.** Let $F$ be a field and $\xi\in F^\times$ with finite quantum
characteristic $e=e(F,\xi)\in\{2,3,\dots\}$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). We work in
the NONDEGENERATE branch $\xi\ne1$; then $\xi$ is a primitive $e$-th root of
unity in $F$, and all statements on this page live in one of the two
sub-branches: (C0) $\operatorname{char}F=0$, or (CP)
$\operatorname{char}F=p>0$ with $p\nmid e$. The Hecke parameter is written
$\xi$ here; it is the letter $q$ of `def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras`.

**Hecke side.** Fix the level-one fundamental weight $\Lambda_0$ of the cyclic
affine type-$A$ datum with all $d_i=1$ and charge $0$
([[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]). With the conventions of
`def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras`, $H^\Lambda_d=H_{F,\xi}(S_d)$
is the finite type-$A$ Hecke algebra $T_r^2=(\xi-1)T_r+\xi$
(`prop-cyclotomic-hecke-algebras-of-level-one-are-finite-hecke-algebras`), and
$H^\Lambda_\alpha=e_\alpha H^\Lambda_d$ are its residue-content blocks
(`def-residue-sequence-idempotents-and-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks`).

**KLR side.** Use the type-$A$ specialization $Q^A$ of
`def-type-a-cyclotomic-specialization-of-the-qg-klr-algebras` with the same $e$
and the STANDARD homogeneous first-strand cyclotomic quotient

Over any field $F$ in the charged finite-$e$ conventions, the explicit maps
$$\rho\colon R^\Lambda_\alpha\to H^\Lambda_\alpha,\qquad \sigma\colon H^\Lambda_\alpha\to R^\Lambda_\alpha$$
from [[lem-hecke-intertwiners-produce-local-klr-generators]] and

summing over the finite height-$d$ contents gives
$$H^\Lambda_d\cong\bigoplus_\alpha R^\Lambda_\alpha .$$
On idempotents the maps are the literal identity, and the dot image is
$x_r-i_r$ in the degenerate branch and $1-q_H^{-i_r}X_r$ in the nondegenerate
branch. This result precedes the late dimension, basis and primitive-block

derivations.claim: **The integer lattice and its spanning forms.** The KLR presentation is defined over $\mathbb Z$ and its relations involve only integer coefficients [F3]; ordered dot monomials, crossing words and word idempotents give normal forms that straighten with integer structure constants. In the finite characteristic-zero quotient the dots are nilpotent (the relations force bounded dot powers in every position), so only finitely many normal forms are nonzero in each block; their $\mathbb Z$-span $H^\Lambda_\alpha(\mathbb Z)$ is therefore a finitely generated torsion-free $\mathbb Z$-module, closed under multiplication, and the homogeneous degrees of the generators induce its grading.

**Base change from K.** Put $L=H^\Lambda_\alpha(\mathbb Z)$ and let $C_{\mathbb Q}$ be the rational KLR presentation. Its generator map $C_{\mathbb Q}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}L$ is surjective by [F3]. Extending to $K$ gives the composition $C_K\twoheadrightarrow K\otimes_{\mathbb Z}L\twoheadrightarrow H^\Lambda_\alpha(K)$, with the second arrow induced by the inclusion of $L$. Both arrows are surjective because their named generators generate the targets, and their composition is the generator-matching all-sector isomorphism of [F2]; therefore both arrows are isomorphisms. Faithful scalar extension from $\mathbb Q$ to $K$ also proves the rational generator map is an isomorphism, without requiring a Hecke root of unity in $\mathbb Q$. Hence the lattice has rank $\dim_KH^\Lambda_\alpha(K)$ and the first base-change map is an isomorphism of graded algebras.

**Reduction modulo p is surjective, including zero sectors.** Let $F$ be a field of sub-branch (CP) with a primitive $e$-th root of unity, and put $C_F=R^\Lambda_\alpha(F)$ for the cyclotomic KLR presentation. Its generators map onto $F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}L$ because the generators of $L$ satisfy the integer presentation relations [F3]. The all-sector theorem [F2] identifies $H^\Lambda_\alpha(F)$ with $C_F$, so composing gives a generator-matching graded surjection $H^\Lambda_\alpha(F)\twoheadrightarrow F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}L$ for every content. If $H^\Lambda_\alpha(F)=0$, that theorem gives $C_F=0$, and the surjection forces $F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}L=0$; since $L$ is free of rank $\dim_KH^\Lambda_\alpha(K)$ by step 1.2, the characteristic-zero sector is also zero. In all cases $\dim_FH^\Lambda_\alpha(F)\ge\dim_KH^\Lambda_\alpha(K)$. Thus no nonzero-support premise or prior cross-characteristic support assertion is needed.

**Dimension comparison.** Both sides are graded algebras spanned by the finitely many normal forms of rank $d$, and the total dimension over all contents of rank $d$ equals $l^dd!$ in every field of the regime, by the PBW basis and dimension statement [F4]. Summing the individual inequalities of step 2.1 over the finitely many contents of rank $d$ therefore forces equality for every content; each surjection is an isomorphism of graded algebras. Its inverse is the generator-matching map from the tensor lattice asserted in the Definition. The result includes zero sectors and rank zero, where both sides are the ground field with their singleton unit, and level zero at positive rank, where both sides are the zero quotient.

**No choice.** The lattice is the span of explicit normal forms, and the base-change maps are checked by a finite dimension count over finitely many contents; no family of nonempty sets is selected. Hence no choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

Work in the regime of
[[def-nondegenerate-root-of-unity-level-one-hecke-regime]]. Fix a partition
$\mu$, put $d=|\mu|$, $\alpha=\operatorname{cont}(\mu)$, and let $K(\mu)$ be
the $F$-span of the Murphy elements $m_{S,T}$ of
[[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]] with
$S,T$ standard tableaux of a multipartition strictly dominating $\mu$; by
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]] $K(\mu)$ is a
two-sided ideal of $H^\Lambda_d$ and $z_\mu:=m_{t^\mu t^\mu}+K(\mu)$ is
defined. Define the (level-one) **cell/Specht module**
$$S(\mu):=H^\Lambda_d\,z_\mu\subseteq H^\Lambda_d/K(\mu),$$
a LEFT $H^\Lambda_d$-module lying in the block $H^\Lambda_\alpha$.

For every standard $\mu$-tableau $T$
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]) fix a reduced decomposition
$w_T=s_{r_1}\cdots s_{r_m}$ of the associated permutation and put
$z_T:=T_{w_T}z_\mu$, $v_T:=\psi_{w_T}z_\mu$ in the Khovanov--Lauda presentation
of `def-type-a-cyclotomic-specialization-of-the-qg-klr-algebras`. For a
removable $i$-node $A$ of a partition $\lambda$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) define
$$d_A(\lambda):=\#\{\text{addable }i\text{-nodes strictly below }A\}-\#\{\text{removable }i\text{-nodes strictly below }A\}$$
(equivalently in the level-one symmetric residue convention of the regime) and
define the **degree** of a standard tableau inductively by
$\deg(\varnothing):=0$ and, for $d>0$,
$\deg(T):=\deg(T_{\le d-1})+d_A(\mu)$ where $A$ is the node of $T$ containing
$d$.

The definition asserts, and
`thm-graded-specht-module-has-homogeneous-tableau-basis` on this page proves,
that $\{v_T:T\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is a homogeneous $F$-basis of
$S(\mu)$ making it a graded $R^\Lambda_\alpha$-module whose $q$-character is
$\operatorname{ch}_qS(\mu)=\sum_Tq^{\deg T}i_T$; forgetting the grading
recovers the ungraded cell module. **Convention.** This is the LEFT Murphy cell
module, obtained from the right cellular datum by $h\cdot m=m h^*$. Forgetting
its grading, `thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual`
identifies it with the star-contragredient dual of the same-shape
independently defined ordinary Dipper--James Specht module $P(\mu)$. Separately,
`thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell` gives
$S(\mu)\cong P(\mu')^{\theta}$ after the same left-module conversion. These are
two proved module comparisons, not the identification of an untwisted conjugate
module. The sign pullback may change ordinary residue content from $-\alpha$ to
$\alpha$; these ungraded comparisons do not assert homogeneity of the ordinary
form or of a raw Hecke sign automorphism in the fixed transported grading. The
labelling of simples by $e$-restricted or $e$-regular partitions is NOT asserted
here; it is determined by the head-classification theorem later on this page.

No choice is used in the definition.

Fix an integer $e\ge 2$ and put $I:=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z=\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$
with its cyclic order; elements of $I$ are called **residues**. Let
$A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ be the integer matrix with

$$a_{ii}=2,\qquad a_{i,i-1}=a_{i,i+1}=-1\ \ (i\in I)$$

when $e\ge 3$, and with $a_{00}=a_{11}=2$ and the single double edge
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ when $e=2$; all indices are read modulo $e$. Thus for
$e\ge3$ all off-diagonal entries other than the neighbouring entries $-1$ are
$0$, and for $e=2$ the matrix is
$\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$. Take the diagonal symmetrizer
$D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\dots,1)$ and the quantum parameter $q$ over
$\mathbb Q$, so that $q_i=q^{d_i}=q$ for every $i\in I$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]).

Choose free abelian groups

$$P=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\Lambda_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z\delta, \qquad P^{\vee}=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z h_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z d,$$

with the $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times
P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$ determined by

$$\langle\Lambda_j,h_i\rangle=\delta_{ij},\qquad \langle\delta,h_i\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\Lambda_j,d\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\delta,d\rangle=1 .$$

For $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $\lambda\in P$, also use the transposed notation
$\langle h,\lambda\rangle:=\langle\lambda,h\rangle$. This notation pairs
a coweight with a weight and is distinct from the symmetric weight form below.

Define the **simple roots**

$$\alpha_i:=\sum_{j\in I}a_{ji}\Lambda_j+\delta_{i0}\,\delta\qquad(i\in I),$$

let $Q:=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\alpha_i\subseteq P$ be the **root lattice**
and $Q^+$ its nonnegative cone, and define the **central element**
$c:=\sum_{i\in I}h_i\in P^{\vee}$. The **level** of $\lambda\in P$ is
$\langle c,\lambda\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ ([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]),
and the **classical weight lattice** is $P_{\mathrm{cl}}:=P/\mathbb Z\delta$.

The **diagram reflection** $\tau$ is the pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear
involutions $\tau:P\to P$, $P^{\vee}\to P^{\vee}$ with
$\tau(\Lambda_i)=\Lambda_{-i}$, $\tau(\delta)=\delta$, $\tau(h_i)=h_{-i}$ and
$\tau(d)=d$ (indices negated in $\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$).

The **normalized affine weight form** is the symmetric $\mathbb Q$-bilinear form on $P_{\mathbb Q}:=P\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ determined, in the decomposition $P_{\mathbb Q}=Q_{\mathbb Q}\oplus\mathbb Q\Lambda_0$, by

$$(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)=a_{ij},\qquad (\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)=\delta_{i0},\qquad (\Lambda_0,\Lambda_0)=0.$$

Thus, for $x=\sum_i x_i\alpha_i$, $y=\sum_i y_i\alpha_i$ and $t,s\in\mathbb Q$, set

$$(x+t\Lambda_0,y+s\Lambda_0)=\sum_{i,j}x_i a_{ij}y_j+t y_0+s x_0.$$

In particular $(\lambda,\alpha_i)=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle$ and $(\lambda,\delta)=\langle\lambda,c\rangle$. Its restriction to $Q$ is integer-valued; on all of $P$ it is rational-valued. This form on weights is distinct from the weight-coweight pairing. Define $s_i(\lambda):=\lambda-\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\alpha_i$ and let $W$ be the group generated by these simple reflections; the form is $W$-invariant and $\tau$-invariant.

For a realization as in [[def-realization-of-a-generalized-cartan-matrix]], set $Q=\bigoplus_{i=1}^n\mathbb Z\alpha_i$ and $Q^+=\bigoplus_{i=1}^n\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$. Define $\operatorname{ht}(\sum_i k_i\alpha_i)=\sum_i k_i$. For $\lambda,\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ write $\mu\le\lambda$ if $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$.

Independence of the simple roots makes coordinates unique. Thus $Q^+\cap(-Q^+)=\{0\}$, which proves antisymmetry of the order; closure under addition proves transitivity, and $0\in Q^+$ proves reflexivity. Positive roots will belong to $Q^+\setminus\{0\}$, not all of $Q^+$.

Retain English Young diagrams, an $l$-multicomposition $\mu$ of $d$, its
diagram, and the row-reading initial standard tableau $t^\mu$, in which
$1,2,\dots,d$ appear in order along the successive rows from top to bottom
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]); for a single
component this is the standard tableau of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]. A $\mu$-tableau $T$ is a
placement of $1,\dots,d$ in the nodes of $\mu$. It is **row-strict** if its
entries increase from left to right in every row of every component, and
**standard** if it is row- and column-strict. The group $S_d$ acts on tableaux
by its action on entries, and for a $\mu$-tableau $T$ the permutation $w_T$ is
defined by $w_Tt^\mu=T$. The **strong Bruhat order** on tableaux is
$$S\le_BT\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad w_S\le w_T$$
in the Bruhat order of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], identified
with its one-based realization as in
[[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]. We write $S\unlhd T$
for $S\le_BT$ and $S\lhd T$ for strict order; the separately declared meaning
of $\unrhd$ on partitions ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) is not
reused for tableaux. On row-strict $S,T$ the order $\unlhd$ is equivalent to
the prefix-shape comparison
$$\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le a})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le a})\quad\text{for every }a,$$
where $T^{\le a}$ erases the nodes occupied by entries $>a$ and
$\operatorname{sh}$ records the resulting row lengths read in row-reading
order; this row-sequence dominance is distinct from the weak Bruhat order and
must not be reversed. The transposition criterion is
$$S=(a_1\,b_1)\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$$
with $a_n<b_n$ and $b_n$ occupying an earlier row-reading node than $a_n$ in
$(a_{n+1}\,b_{n+1})\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$ for each $n$.

For entries $r,s$ of one component define $r\to_Ts$ if they lie in the same row
and $s$ is strictly to the right of $r$; $r\downarrow_Ts$ if they lie in the
same column and $s$ is strictly below $r$; and $r\nearrow_Ts$ if $s$ is
strictly above and strictly right of $r$ (south-west is the reverse of
$\nearrow_T$). A **weak Bruhat graph edge** $T\xrightarrow{r}S$ requires both
tableaux standard, $S=s_rT$, and $r$ occupying an earlier row-reading node
than $r+1$. Equivalently $r+1\nearrow_Tr$, or $r$ lies in an earlier component
than $r+1$. In particular a same-row or same-column swap is NOT a standard
edge. A **terminal path** is a directed path in this graph, and $T$ is
$(r_1,\dots,r_m)$-**terminal** if there are standard tableaux
$S_1\xrightarrow{r_1}S_2\xrightarrow{r_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{r_m}T$.

The **Garnir belt** at a node $(a,b,n)$ with $(a+1,b,n)$ also a node of $\mu$
consists of the nodes $(a,c,n)$ for $b\le c\le\mu_a$ and the nodes
$(a+1,g,n)$ for $1\le g\le b$. The **Garnir tableau** of shape $\mu$ at
$(a,b,n)$ is the unique maximal standard $\mu$-tableau in the order $\unlhd$
among the standard $\mu$-tableaux agreeing with $t^\mu$ outside the
$(a,b,n)$-Garnir belt; it equals $t^\mu$ in the degenerate case
$b=1=\mu_a$. A **horizontal brick** is a string of consecutive entries along
same-row right arrows. For the vertical exceptional-prefix and terminal assertions assume that
$\mu$ is a multipartition; the rank, prefix-order and row-sorting assertions
allow multicompositions. The following source facts are retained with these
exact conventions and are proved below: the transposition criterion and the
prefix-shape criterion; the row-strictness of a vertical consecutive swap and
its exceptional-prefix comparison; agreement outside the Garnir belt for
tableaux below a Garnir tableau; and the four terminal alternatives for a
horizontal or vertical consecutive pair, the last alternative being $t^\mu$
for a horizontal pair and the corresponding Garnir tableau for a vertical

derivations.claim: **Counting addable and removable nodes (1).** Deleting the removable node $A$ of residue $i$ makes $A$ addable. Apart from this change, all corner changes occur immediately next to $A$ and have residues $i-1$ or $i+1$, which differ from $i$ since $e\ge2$ (for $e=2$ the two neighbor residues coincide with each other). Hence the signed count of $i$-nodes strictly above $A$ is unchanged, as is the signed count strictly below it. There is no other addable or removable $i$-node in the row of $A$. Splitting the signed corner count of $\mu$ into its above and below parts and the removable node $A$ therefore gives $d_A(\mu)+d^A(\mu^A)=d_i(\mu)+1$.

**The Cartan formula (2).** Write $u_j$ for the basis vector indexed by $j\in\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ in the free abelian group on residues, and choose $R$ greater than the number of nonzero rows of $\mu$. Put $b_r=\mu_r-r$. The signed corner vector is $\sum_i d_i(\mu)u_i=u_{-R}+\sum_{r=1}^R(u_{b_r+1}-u_{b_r})$: adjacent row-boundary terms cancel precisely when the corresponding node is not a corner, and the tail term cancels the artificial bottom boundary. For the empty partition this telescopes to $u_0$, so $d_i(\varnothing)=\delta_{i,0}=(\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)$. Adding a node of residue $j$ moves one $b_r=j-1$ to $j$ and changes this vector by $u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}$. Thus each $d_i$ changes by $-a_{ij}$, including the double neighbor contribution when $e=2$. The vector with coordinates $(\Lambda_0-\alpha,\alpha_i)$ has the same initial value and the same change when $\alpha$ increases by $\alpha_j$. Induction on the number of nodes proves (2).

**Bricks in the first row (5)(i).** All nodes carrying $m,\ldots,d$ lie consecutively in one row, by [F4] and standardness; since they are the largest entries, they form the rightmost segment of that row. At every addition in the codegree recursion for a brick in row one, there are no rows strictly above, so the increment is zero. Summing these increments proves $\operatorname{codeg}(T)=\operatorname{codeg}(T_{\le m-1})$.

**The defect recursion (3).** Expanding, $\operatorname{def}(\alpha)-\operatorname{def}(\alpha-\alpha_i)=(\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)-((\alpha,\alpha)-(\alpha-\alpha_i,\alpha-\alpha_i))/2=(\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)-(\alpha,\alpha_i)+(\alpha_i,\alpha_i)/2=d_i(\mu)+1$ by (2) and $(\alpha_i,\alpha_i)=2$, which is the displayed recursion [F3].

**Degree plus codegree (4).** For $d=0$ both definitions give $0=\operatorname{def}(0)$. For $d>0$ let $A$ be the node containing $d$ and $i=\operatorname{res}A$; by the induction hypothesis applied to $T_{\le d-1}$ and by step 2.1, $\deg(T)+\operatorname{codeg}(T)=\deg(T_{\le d-1})+\operatorname{codeg}(T_{\le d-1})+d_A(\mu)+d^A(\mu^A)=\operatorname{def}(\alpha-\alpha_i)+d_i(\mu)+1=\operatorname{def}(\alpha)$, where the middle equality uses (1) [F2, F3].

**Full residue bricks (5)(ii).** Suppose the terminal brick has $e$ nodes in row $r$ and occupies columns $c+1,\ldots,c+e$. Put $\lambda=T_{\le m-1}$. If $r=1$, step 1.3 applies. If $r>1$, standardness implies that all nodes in rows above $r$ already occur in $\lambda$ and that $\lambda_{r-1}\ge c+e$: each entry above a brick node is smaller, and all entries outside the terminal brick are at most $m-1$. Immediately before each of the $e$ additions, row $r$ therefore has length strictly smaller than $\lambda_{r-1}$. The signed corner counts strictly above row $r$ stay fixed throughout these pre-addition shapes. Indeed, in the top $r-1$ rows each maximal plateau of equal row lengths contributes one addable node at the start of its first row and one removable node at the end of its last row, and the last such row remains removable because its length is greater than that of row $r$ before the addition. Thus the number of addable corners above the brick equals the number of removable corners above it. The brick residues $(c+1-r),\ldots,(c+e-r)$ run through $I$ once. Summing the codegree increment for these residues counts each of the fixed above addable corners once positively and each above removable corner once negatively, giving zero. Hence the codegrees before and after the brick agree. The boundary count, defect recursion and tableau induction establish all five clauses by finite computations and use no choice.

Retain English Young diagrams, an $l$-multicomposition $\mu$ of $d$, its
diagram, and the row-reading initial standard tableau $t^\mu$, in which
$1,2,\dots,d$ appear in order along the successive rows from top to bottom
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]); for a single
component this is the standard tableau of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]. A $\mu$-tableau $T$ is a
placement of $1,\dots,d$ in the nodes of $\mu$. It is **row-strict** if its
entries increase from left to right in every row of every component, and
**standard** if it is row- and column-strict. The group $S_d$ acts on tableaux
by its action on entries, and for a $\mu$-tableau $T$ the permutation $w_T$ is
defined by $w_Tt^\mu=T$. The **strong Bruhat order** on tableaux is
$$S\le_BT\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad w_S\le w_T$$
in the Bruhat order of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], identified
with its one-based realization as in
[[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]. We write $S\unlhd T$
for $S\le_BT$ and $S\lhd T$ for strict order; the separately declared meaning
of $\unrhd$ on partitions ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) is not
reused for tableaux. On row-strict $S,T$ the order $\unlhd$ is equivalent to
the prefix-shape comparison
$$\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le a})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le a})\quad\text{for every }a,$$
where $T^{\le a}$ erases the nodes occupied by entries $>a$ and
$\operatorname{sh}$ records the resulting row lengths read in row-reading
order; this row-sequence dominance is distinct from the weak Bruhat order and
must not be reversed. The transposition criterion is
$$S=(a_1\,b_1)\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$$
with $a_n<b_n$ and $b_n$ occupying an earlier row-reading node than $a_n$ in
$(a_{n+1}\,b_{n+1})\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$ for each $n$.

For entries $r,s$ of one component define $r\to_Ts$ if they lie in the same row
and $s$ is strictly to the right of $r$; $r\downarrow_Ts$ if they lie in the
same column and $s$ is strictly below $r$; and $r\nearrow_Ts$ if $s$ is
strictly above and strictly right of $r$ (south-west is the reverse of
$\nearrow_T$). A **weak Bruhat graph edge** $T\xrightarrow{r}S$ requires both
tableaux standard, $S=s_rT$, and $r$ occupying an earlier row-reading node
than $r+1$. Equivalently $r+1\nearrow_Tr$, or $r$ lies in an earlier component
than $r+1$. In particular a same-row or same-column swap is NOT a standard
edge. A **terminal path** is a directed path in this graph, and $T$ is
$(r_1,\dots,r_m)$-**terminal** if there are standard tableaux
$S_1\xrightarrow{r_1}S_2\xrightarrow{r_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{r_m}T$.

The **Garnir belt** at a node $(a,b,n)$ with $(a+1,b,n)$ also a node of $\mu$
consists of the nodes $(a,c,n)$ for $b\le c\le\mu_a$ and the nodes
$(a+1,g,n)$ for $1\le g\le b$. The **Garnir tableau** of shape $\mu$ at
$(a,b,n)$ is the unique maximal standard $\mu$-tableau in the order $\unlhd$
among the standard $\mu$-tableaux agreeing with $t^\mu$ outside the
$(a,b,n)$-Garnir belt; it equals $t^\mu$ in the degenerate case
$b=1=\mu_a$. A **horizontal brick** is a string of consecutive entries along
same-row right arrows. For the vertical exceptional-prefix and terminal assertions assume that
$\mu$ is a multipartition; the rank, prefix-order and row-sorting assertions
allow multicompositions. The following source facts are retained with these
exact conventions and are proved below: the transposition criterion and the
prefix-shape criterion; the row-strictness of a vertical consecutive swap and
its exceptional-prefix comparison; agreement outside the Garnir belt for
tableaux below a Garnir tableau; and the four terminal alternatives for a
horizontal or vertical consecutive pair, the last alternative being $t^\mu$
for a horizontal pair and the corresponding Garnir tableau for a vertical
pair. No choice.

In the situation of
[[def-graded-specht-module-by-homogeneous-standard-tableaux]], define
$d^A(\lambda)$ for an ADDABLE $i$-node $A$ to be the number of addable
$i$-nodes strictly ABOVE $A$ minus the number of removable $i$-nodes strictly
ABOVE $A$. Define the codegree of a standard tableau $T$ by
$\operatorname{codeg}(\varnothing):=0$ and
$\operatorname{codeg}(T):=d^A(\mu^A)+\operatorname{codeg}(T_{\le d-1})$, where
$A$ is the node containing $d$ and $\mu^A=\mu\setminus A$. Define the defect of
a residue content $\alpha\in Q_+$ by
$\operatorname{def}(\alpha):=(\Lambda_0,\alpha)-(\alpha,\alpha)/2$ (the
symmetric form of [[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]). Then for every
partition $\mu$ with content $\alpha$ and every standard $\mu$-tableau $T$:

1. $d_A(\mu)+d^A(\mu^A)=d_i(\mu)+1$ where $i$ is the residue of the removable
node $A$ and
$d_i(\mu)=\#\{\text{addable }i\text{-nodes of }\mu\}-\#\{\text{removable }i\text{-nodes of }\mu\}$;

2. $d_i(\mu)=(\Lambda_0-\alpha,\alpha_i)$;

3. $\operatorname{def}(\alpha)=\operatorname{def}(\alpha-\alpha_i)+d_i(\mu)+1$;

4. $\deg(T)+\operatorname{codeg}(T)=\operatorname{def}(\alpha)$;

5. removing a brick does not change the codegree: if
$m\to_Tm+1\to_T\cdots\to_Td$ and $S=T_{\le m-1}$, then
$\operatorname{codeg}(S)=\operatorname{codeg}(T)$ whenever (i) $m,\dots,d$
occupy nodes in the first row of the first component of $T$, or (ii)
$d-m+1=e$ (the quantum characteristic).

No choice is used.

Let $F,q,e,I,\Lambda,\lambda_i$ be as in
[[def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras]]
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]],
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]). On the cyclic affine type-A Cartan
datum take the normalized symmetrizers $d_i=1$ and define the **type-A KLR
datum** $Q^{\mathrm A}$ by
$$Q^{\mathrm A}_{ii}=0,\qquad Q^{\mathrm A}_{ij}=1\quad\text{if }a_{ij}=0,$$
$$Q^{\mathrm A}_{i,i+1}(u,v)=v-u,\qquad Q^{\mathrm A}_{i+1,i}(u,v)=u-v\qquad(e\ge3),$$
$$Q^{\mathrm A}_{01}(u,v)=Q^{\mathrm A}_{10}(u,v)=-(u-v)^2\qquad(e=2).$$
Write $R_\alpha$ for the resulting generalized KLR algebra over $F$
([[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]],
[[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]]) and $R^\Lambda_\alpha$ for
the standard cyclotomic quotient of
[[def-cyclotomic-klr-quotient-at-a-dominant-weight]] (monic first-strand
relations $x_1^{\lambda_{i_1}}e(\nu)=0$).

**The specialization dictionary.** Put $y_r:=x_r$ and $\psi_r:=-\tau_r$. With
these normalizations, the relations (1.6)–(1.15) of the source hold in
$R^\Lambda_\alpha$, and conversely the quotient presented by those relations
is the same algebra; in other words $R^\Lambda_\alpha$ is the sign-modified
cyclotomic Khovanov–Lauda algebra of the source for the cyclic quiver of
quantum characteristic $e$. The verification of the dictionary is elementary
and is recorded here so that no hidden convention is imported:

1. **(Q1)–(Q4).** Non-adjacent pairs have $a_{ij}=0$ and
   $Q^{\mathrm A}_{ij}=1$, homogeneous of degree $0$. For an adjacent pair
   $(i,i+1)$ with $e\ge3$ one has $b_{ij}=a_{ij}=-1$, and $v-u$ is homogeneous
   of degree $2=-2b_{ij}$ with nonzero extremal coefficients of
   $u^{-a_{ij}}=u$ and $v^{-a_{ji}}=v$; the opposite orientation is the
   transpose, so (Q2) is built into the two formulae. For $e=2$ the pair
   $\{0,1\}$ has $a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ and $b_{01}=-2$, and $-(u-v)^2$ is
   symmetric, homogeneous of degree $4=-2b_{01}$, with top coefficient $-1\ne0$.
2. **Dot sliding.** Relation (1.8) comes from $\tau_re(i)=e(s_ri)\tau_r$;
   relations (1.12)–(1.13) reduce to the dot-sliding constants
   $\tau_ax_a-x_{a+1}\tau_a=e(\nu)$ and
   $\tau_ax_{a+1}-x_a\tau_a=-e(\nu)$ on equal colours, whose sign changes to
   the source's constants $+1$ under $\psi=-\tau$.
3. **Quadratic and braid relations.** Relation (1.14): equal colours give
   $\tau^2=Q_{ii}=0$; non-adjacent colours give $\tau^2=1=e(i)$; a forward
   arrow gives $\tau^2=v-u$, evaluated at $(y_r,y_{r+1})$ as
   $y_{r+1}-y_r$; a backward arrow gives $y_r-y_{r+1}$; the $e=2$ double edge
   gives $(y_{r+1}-y_r)(y_r-y_{r+1})$. Relation (1.15): the divided-difference
   numerator
   $\bigl[Q^{\mathrm A}(x_a,x_{a+1})-Q^{\mathrm A}(x_{a+2},x_{a+1})\bigr]/(x_{a+2}-x_a)$
   equals $\pm1$ in the two single-edge cases with $i_{r+2}=i_r$, equals
   $y_r+y_{r+2}-2y_{r+1}$ in the $e=2$ double-edge case, and vanishes
   otherwise; the global sign $\psi=-\tau$ matches the source's three cases.
   The product order is explicit: the source difference is
   $\psi_r\psi_{r+1}\psi_r-\psi_{r+1}\psi_r\psi_{r+1}$, which under
   $\psi=-\tau$ equals the native reversed-word difference
   $\tau_{r+1}\tau_r\tau_{r+1}-\tau_r\tau_{r+1}\tau_r$; for
   $Q=-(u-v)^2$ the displayed quotient is $u+w-2v$. Thus no braid-order sign
   is suppressed, also in characteristic two.

Degrees of products are read on the successive permuted colour pairs as in
[[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]]. This definition introduces
no new basis, trace or primitive-block assertion, and uses no choice
principle.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

derivations.claim: **One edge (1).** Delete entries greater than $r+1$ from both tableaux. These occupy the same nodes and have equal degree-recursion contributions, so they cancel and we may assume $r=d-1$. Write $A$ for the node of $d$ in $T$ and $B$ for the node of $d-1$. In a weak edge $B$ is above $A$, and removing $B$ does not change the boundary counts strictly below $A$. Expanding the two recursions therefore gives $\deg S-\deg T=d_B(\mu)-d_B(\mu\setminus A)$. Removing the $i$-node $A$ changes the addable-minus-removable $j$-node count below $B$ by $a_{ji}$: when $i=j$ one loses a removable node and gains an addable one, giving $2$; at a single edge one loses one addable $j$-node or gains one removable $j$-node, giving $-1$; at $e=2$ the two adjacent colors coincide and the two contributions give $-2$; otherwise it gives zero. Thus $d_B(\mu\setminus A)-d_B(\mu)=a_{ji}$ and the desired difference is $-a_{ji}$.

**Reduced words (2).** The KLR element $\psi_{r_1}\cdots\psi_{r_m}e(i_{t^\mu})$ is homogeneous of degree $\sum_l(-a_{j_l,k_l})$, where $(j_l,k_l)$ is the residue pair at the crossing after the generators to its right have acted, and the reduced word moves $t^\mu$ to $T$ by successive weak edges. Indeed, read the word from right to left: each consecutive-value swap increases inversion length by one and changes only the relative order of its two occupied nodes. No such inversion can be removed along a reduced word, so every inverted node pair also occurs in the final tableau. Nodes comparable along a row or column have the same increasing order in $t^\mu$ and $T$, so no intermediate tableau reverses them; each intermediate tableau is therefore standard. Thus by step 1.1 each edge changes the degree by the negative of the corresponding Cartan coefficient $a_{i_ri_{r+1}}=\deg\psi_re(i)$ [F3]. Summing over the $m$ edges gives $\deg(T)-\deg(t^\mu)=\deg(\psi_{r_1}\cdots\psi_{r_m}e(i_{t^\mu}))$, independent of the word because the degree is a function of $T$ [F2, F3].

**The Garnir exchange (3).** By [F1], $S$ and $T$ agree outside the belt. The prefix shapes immediately before and after the belt coincide for $S,T$, so the outside-label contributions coincide. For belt labels, the rows strictly above its upper row are fixed. Their contribution to each upper-row addition depends only on that node's column, so the sum over the fixed upper-tail node set is identical. For a lower-row addition, subtract the local signed corners of the upper belt row from the actual above-node count. This leaves a fixed external signed-corner count: if the upper row reaches the length of the preceding row, the lost external removable corner and the suppressed local addable corner have exactly the same residue, so their changes cancel in this difference. The sum of that fixed correction over the lower-prefix node set is therefore identical as well. Thus outer contributions cancel in the codegree difference. Translate the belt row indices and residues to the two-row diagram $(m,b)$ with Garnir node $(1,b)$; the calculations below give these residual codegrees. The initial upper head has entries $1,\ldots,b-1$. The Garnir filling puts $b,\ldots,2b-2$ in the lower prefix, $r=2b-1$ at the upper node $(1,b)$, $r+1=2b$ at the lower node $(2,b)$, and the remaining entries along the upper tail. If $e=0$, the upper-belt contents $b-1,\ldots,m-1$ and lower-belt contents $-1,\ldots,b-2$ are disjoint, with each integer appearing once. Consequently the prescribed residue sequence $i_S=i_{s_rT}$ forces every belt label to occupy exactly its node in $s_rT$. That filling has $r+1$ above $r$ in column $b$, so is not standard. Thus no $S$ in the hypothesis exists for $e=0$; clause (3) is vacuous in that extension, without assigning a codegree to a nonexistent standard tableau. Now let $e\ge2$ be finite, and write $\delta_e(t)=1$ if $e\mid t$ and $0$ otherwise. In any standard two-row filling, a lower-row brick occupying columns $p,\ldots,q$ while the upper row has fixed length $x$ contributes $\sum_{c=p}^q(\delta_e(x-c+2)-\delta_e(x-c+1))=\delta_e(x-p+2)-\delta_e(x-q+1)$ to codegree: the addable upper corner has content $x$, the removable upper corner content $x-1$, and the added lower node content $c-2$. In particular a complete $e$-brick contributes zero, agreeing with [F2]. For $S$, the target belt residue word is the single consecutive run $-1,0,\ldots,m-1$ modulo $e$. Every lower brick starting after an upper brick has first endpoint indicator $1$, by comparing the preceding upper residue $x-1$ with the next lower residue $p-2$. Every lower brick has last endpoint indicator $1$: if followed by an upper brick this follows by comparing $q-2$ with $x$, while if it ends the whole belt then $x=m$, $q=b$, and the final prescribed residue gives $m-b+1\equiv0$. Hence every such brick contributes zero except possibly the initial lower brick, whose first indicator is $\delta_e(b)$ since $x=b-1$ and $p=1$. If $S$ starts instead in the upper row, its first residue forces $b\equiv0$, so the same total follows. Therefore $\operatorname{codeg}(S)=\delta_e(b)-1$. For $T$, the lower-prefix additions at columns $1,\ldots,b-1$ occur with upper length $b-1$ and contribute $\delta_e(b)-\delta_e(1)=\delta_e(b)$; the lower node in column $b$ is then added with upper length $b$, contributing $\delta_e(2)-\delta_e(1)=\delta_e(2)$; all upper additions contribute zero. Thus $\operatorname{codeg}(T)=\delta_e(b)+\delta_e(2)$. The matched residual count table is $$\begin{array}{c|c|r|r|r}e&b\bmod e&\operatorname{codeg}(S)&\operatorname{codeg}(T)&\operatorname{codeg}(T)-\operatorname{codeg}(S)\\\hline e>2&\ne0&-1&0&1\\e>2&0&0&1&1\\e=2&1&-1&1&2\\e=2&0&0&2&2\end{array}.$$ By [F2], degree difference is the reverse codegree difference at fixed shape and content. The vertically adjacent residues at $r,r+1$ are distinct and joined by one edge for $e>2$ and by a double edge for $e=2$; hence every row of the table gives $\deg S-\deg T=-a_{i_ri_{r+1}}$. All signs are accounted for by the explicit addable-minus-removable endpoint count.

**No choice.** The reductions use the finitely many nodes of the two tableaux, the finite belt and its finitely many bricks, and the finitely many residue comparisons; no family of nonempty sets is selected. Hence no choice is used.
